paras: The mock lynching of two Black prisoners at Williston, Florida, took place in Levy County in or before August 1915, when two Black men held on a charge of cow stealing were roped by the neck, hoisted and choked to force them to confess. A local paper, the Williston Courier, first reported that the county sheriff had been seen in the woods trying to lynch the men, but the Ocala Evening Star later called that story a fake and reported that the sheriff blamed men of Williston. The case drew notice in the Florida press chiefly as a dispute over the sheriff's conduct.

The two men lived near Raleigh and were arrested on a charge of cow stealing, after which they were taken to Williston. Their names, the date of their arrest and the outcome of the charge are not given in the coverage.

According to the prisoners, "certain Williston men" took them out and threatened to lynch them if they did not confess. They said they were bound and blindfolded, had ropes put around their necks, and were hauled off the ground and choked two or three times each in an effort to make them implicate themselves or someone else. Both men survived.

The sheriff of Levy County, who is not named, gave his own account of being in the woods with the prisoners. He said he took them there with their consent and with a photographer, and bound them in order to make pictures that he meant to use as evidence against the men who had given them "the third degree."

The sheriff produced affidavits from the men concerned that supported his account and stated that the prisoners had been treated with "extreme cruelty" by Williston men. No report of arrests, charges or an investigation of the Williston men appears in the coverage.

The episode reached the wider press through the Ocala Evening Star, which on 23 August 1915 summarized the Courier's story of the sheriff "attempting to lynch a couple of negroes." The Star called it "a plain case, cne [one] way or the other": if true, the sheriff should be dismissed, and if false, he should sue the Courier for criminal libel.

On 3 September the Star reversed course, calling the Courier story a fake "like most of the stories in that sheet" while still printing the prisoners' description of being choked. The Lakeland Evening Telegram reprinted that paragraph on 8 September under the headline "A Slander on Sheriff of Levy County." Both papers framed the matter around the sheriff's reputation rather than the treatment of the prisoners, and no Black-press coverage was found.

The accounts disagree on who roped the prisoners: the Williston Courier, as relayed by the Star, placed the sheriff at an attempted lynching, while the prisoners and the sheriff's affidavits named Williston men. The Courier's own text was not found, and the case against its version rests on the sheriff's statement and the affidavits he produced.

bases: Two Black prisoners accused of cow stealing said Williston men threatened to lynch them, put ropes around their necks and hoisted them off the ground to force a confession, a threatened (mock) lynching; no one was killed (A2).

No one was killed: the two men were choked and threatened with lynching to make them confess to cow stealing (A2); the attackers are 'certain Williston men' of unstated number, or the sheriff in the Courier version (A1).

The Williston Courier story, known only through the Ocala Star (A1), put the sheriff at the scene of an attempted lynching; the Star later called it a fake and gave the prisoners' and the sheriff's versions, which blame Williston men (A2).
